Objectives

  • Define common terminology related to neoplasia and malignant transformation
  • Differentiate benign from malignant tumors and describe the major mechanisms of local invasion and metastatic spread.
  • Explain the basic principles of cancer diagnosis, grading, and TNM staging.
  • Describe the principles and different roles of surgery in cancer management, including curative, diagnostic, prophylactic, cytoreductive, and palliative surgery.
  • Differentiate neoadjuvant, adjuvant, systemic, radiation, and local/regional therapies and explain how they are integrated within multidisciplinary cancer care.
Notes

Surgical Oncology

Exam focus: terminology and core concepts from the lecture slides, more than cancer-specific staging detail.

Basic Terminology

  • Neoplasia: new tissue growth that is unregulated, irreversible, and monoclonal.
  • These features distinguish it from hyperplasia and repair.
  • Hyperplasia: increased number of cells
  • Hypertrophy: increased cell size
  • Metaplasia: replacement of one differentiated cell type by another
  • Dysplasia: abnormal cellular growth and maturation
  • Neoplasia: autonomous abnormal proliferation
  • Premalignant polyp = adenomatous (not hamartomatous, inflammatory or hyperplastic). 427
Notes

1. Cellular Adaptation & Neoplasia

ProcessDefinitionKey point
Hypertrophy↑ cell size, no change in cell numberCardiac hypertrophy in chronic hypertension (persistent ↑ pressure/resistance)
Hyperplasia↑ cell number, usually a regulated stimulus (e.g. estrogen/androgen)Regulated and reversible once stimulus removed — unlike neoplasia
NeoplasiaUnregulated, irreversible tissue growthUsually monoclonal — one mutated cell accumulates further mutations over years
MetaplasiaReplacement of one differentiated cell type by another differentiated typeBarrett esophagus: squamous → columnar (chronic acid reflux)
DysplasiaAbnormal/disordered proliferation with cytologic atypia (pleomorphism)End result of persistent metaplasia; premalignant if stimulus persists
HIGH-YIELD DISTINCTION
Neoplasm ≠ cancer — a neoplasm may be benign or malignant. Example: lipoma is a benign neoplasm with essentially no invasion/metastasis risk.
DO NOT CONFUSE
Carcinoma in situ: full-thickness dysplasia that remains above the basement membrane.
Invasive carcinoma: malignant cells breach the basement membrane.
Progression does not always follow a fixed normal → hyperplasia → metaplasia → dysplasia → cancer sequence.

Neoplasia Progression

Normal → Metaplasia → Dysplasia → Carcinoma in situ → Invasive carcinoma → Metastasis

Basic Terminology

FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationUsually well differentiatedVariable / poorly differentiated
GrowthUsually slowOften faster
Local invasionNoYes
MetastasisNoPossible
RecurrenceUsually uncommonMay occur
Clinical impactUsually localLocal + systemic
Notes

2. Benign vs Malignant Tumors

BenignMalignant
GrowthUsually slowFaster
InvasionLocalized, no significant invasionLocal invasion
MetastasisEssentially nonePossible distant dissemination
RecurrenceUncommonHigher recurrence & mortality risk
Differentiation
Well differentiated: closely resembles the tissue of origin; origin easily recognized; better prognosis (though dysplastic change can still occur above the basement membrane).
Poorly differentiated: minimal resemblance to origin; special stains may be needed to identify tissue type.
WORST PROGNOSIS
Undifferentiated / anaplastic tumors carry the worst prognosis of the differentiation spectrum.

Carcinogenesis

  • Lung cancer screening → annual low-dose CT for age 50–80 with ≥ 20 pack-years who smoke now or quit within 15 years: e.g. a 52-year-old, 30 pack-years, quit 10 years ago 442 Final; the only candidate among the choices was the 51-year-old with 30 pack-years (others too young or too few pack-years). 441 Final
Notes

3. Carcinogenesis & Cancer Risk Factors

Cancer usually results from multiple accumulated genetic errors, often initiated or promoted by identifiable risk factors.

Risk factorAssociated cancer(s)
BRCA1 / BRCA2 (inherited)Breast / ovarian cancer predisposition
APC mutationEarliest event in the classic adenoma–carcinoma sequence (colorectal cancer)
Processed / smoked dietGI / gastric malignancy
AsbestosMesothelioma
Aromatic dyesBladder cancer
Smoking / alcoholMultiple carcinogenic exposures
Radiation (therapeutic or environmental)Secondary malignancy, often ~20 years later (e.g. angiosarcoma in a previously irradiated field)
HPVCervical & anal cancer — screen
Hepatitis virusesHepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
Hormonal exposureHormone-sensitive malignancies (e.g. prostate)
Increasing age↑ cumulative mutations + ↑ DNA-repair failure
TREND NOTE
Occupational cancers are now less common due to improved workplace safety; late treatment-related malignancies are seen more often because cancer survival has improved.
  • HCC risk factors: cirrhosis, hepatitis B (and C); smoking was keyed as the "except" (least risk) — note hepatitis A does not cause HCC. 426

Genatic Mutation

  • Germline: inherited/heritable predisposition present throughout the body.
  • Somatic: acquired mutation arising in particular cells during life.
  • Germline mutation can arise de novo, with no previous family history.
Notes

4. Somatic vs Germline Mutations

Somatic mutationGermline mutation
LocationOnly within tumor cellsThroughout the body's normal cells
Inherited?Not necessarilyYes — hereditary predisposition
TestingTumor tissue (guides targeted/systemic therapy)Blood or normal tissue, not only tumor
ImplicationInforms treatment selection↑ risk of multiple different cancers
FAMILIAL ADENOMATOUS POLYPOSIS (FAP)
APC mutation + suggestive family history → consider FAP + germline testing. Germline APC → predisposition to colorectal and other tumors (small-bowel, thyroid).
LYNCH SYNDROME
Associated with microsatellite instability (MSI) / MMR deficiency. Predisposes to colorectal plus extracolonic cancers (ovarian, pancreatic) — it is a germline mutation. Strong family history is not always present; a young patient with colorectal cancer should raise suspicion. New colorectal cancers often get routine MSI/MMR testing → abnormal result → consider germline testing.
Notes

DNA Mismatch Repair

Replication errors occur daily. Mismatch-repair (MMR) proteins identify and repair these errors, preventing mutation accumulation. MMR protein deficiency → unrepaired mutations accumulate → progressive genomic instability → cancer development.

1 Clinical indicators for hereditary cancer assessment: young age, suggestive family history, characteristic tumor patterns, syndrome-specific criteria/scores.

1.

  • HCC on cirrhosis within Milan criteria (single ≤5 cm, Child B) → liver transplant. 438 ×3 438

Surgical Oncology

  • Field of surgery concerned with the diagnosis, staging, and surgical management of cancer, integrating surgery with other oncologic therapies to achieve the best cancer and patient outcomes.
  • Risk assessment → Diagnosis → Staging → Treatment planning → Surgery → Adjuvant therapy decisions → Surveillance / Survivorship
Notes

5. Role of Surgical Oncology

Surgical oncology involves far more than performing surgery — management is multidisciplinary from diagnosis onward:

Cancer diagnosis
Risk assessment
Staging
Surgical management
Participation in MDT / tumor board
Integration with medical / radiation oncology
Prevention / risk-reducing surgery
Surveillance after treatment

Surgical Oncology: Prevention

  • Prophylactic Surgery:
  • Surgery may be performed before cancer develops in patients with a sufficiently high cancer risk.
  • FAP → prophylactic colectomy/proctocolectomy
  • BRCA1/BRCA2 → risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy and/or salpingo-

oophorectomy

Notes

6. Cancer Prevention & Risk-Reducing Surgery

Prophylactic / risk-reducing surgery is performed before cancer develops in patients at very high inherited risk — distinct from curative cancer surgery.

EXAMPLES
FAP: prophylactic total colectomy may be required in young patients with extensive polyposis.
BRCA1/BRCA2: risk-reducing surgery can markedly reduce breast/ovarian cancer risk in selected, appropriately counselled patients (BRCA1 carriers have a very high lifetime cancer risk).

Prevention may be surgical and/or medical/hormonal.

  • BRCA1 → breast cancer. 437 ×3 436
  • Screening:
  • Breast → Mammography
  • Cervical → HPV testing ± Pap smear
  • Colorectal → FIT, colonoscopy
  • Prostate → PSA
  • Screening test should be
    • Be sensitive
      • Be specific
      • Be acceptable
      • Detect cancer at a stage when early treatment is beneficial
      • Be cost-effective.
  • Screening = detect cancer in its early stages, when treatment is possible. 439
Notes

7. Cancer Screening

CancerScreening modality
BreastMammography
CervicalPap smear / cervical screening
ColorectalStool-based testing and/or colonoscopy, depending on risk
Colorectal Screening
Colonoscopy is the best modality — highly sensitive/specific and allows simultaneous polypectomy, preventing polyp-to-cancer progression. As a national program its main limitation is cost/resources.
Stool-based testing (average-risk population): detects occult blood → positive → colonoscopy; repeated periodically; false-negatives occur but are rare.
HIGH-RISK SCREENING RULE
First-degree relative with colorectal cancer at age 40 → start colonoscopy around age 30 (10 years earlier than the affected relative).
  • Average-risk colorectal screening (no family history) → colonoscopy every 10 years starting at 45–50. 441 Final
  • 62-year-old with hematochezia and 3rd-degree hemorrhoids → colonoscopy first (rule out cancer before treating the hemorrhoids). 435
  • Breast cancer prognosis depends mainly on the number of positive axillary lymph nodes. 427 429 Final ×2

Surgical Oncology: Diagnosis

  • History and physical examination:
    • Crucial for risk assessment and guidance of therapy
      • Signs and symptoms assessment of:
      • Primary tumor (local)
      • Systemic consequences
      • Metastatic disease
  • Risk factors and family history
  • Functional status
  • Tumor markers
Notes

8. Assessment of a Patient with Suspected Cancer

History

Constitutional/alarm symptoms: weight loss, fever, loss of appetite
Family history
Smoking / alcohol
Previous radiation exposure
Other tumor-specific risk factors
Primary/local symptoms (GI bleeding, dysphagia, breast symptoms, etc.)
Regional/distant symptoms: ascites, jaundice, other metastatic signs
  • 70-year-old with bright red blood mixed with stool, weight loss, constipation, pallor → colon cancer (adenocarcinoma). 436 ×5 430
  • Pancreatic head tumor → CA 19-9. 436
  • Palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) → tumor of the head of the pancreas, not a CBD stone. 427
Notes

Examination

General appearance + performance status (every patient)
Breast palpation
PR/DRE for rectal cancer
Abdominal exam for ascites/masses
Comorbidities & fitness for major surgery/chemo
Curative vs primarily palliative intent
CLASSIC SIGN
Sister Mary Joseph nodule = umbilical metastatic deposit suggesting intra-abdominal malignancy.
  • Locally advanced low rectal cancer (T3N1M0), not obstructed → start with (chemo)radiation (neoadjuvant), not upfront surgery. 437
Notes

9. Initial Workup & Tumor Markers

Workup: history/exam → routine labs → tumor markers (where relevant) → imaging/endoscopy → tissue diagnosis.

Tumor markerAssociation / use
CEAColorectal cancer; baseline/prognostic/follow-up
CA 19-9Pancreatic / biliary malignancy
CA-125Ovarian cancer; may rise with peritoneal carcinomatosis
AFPHepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
PSAProstate cancer
CalcitoninMedullary thyroid carcinoma
ThyroglobulinFollow-up of differentiated thyroid cancer
EXAM TRAP
Tumor markers have different purposes — they are not interchangeable and are not universally diagnostic.
  • Prostate → PSA (also the marker for follow-up after prostate-cancer treatment). 436 439 Final
  • Malignant tumor of the parafollicular C cells = medullary carcinoma (calcitonin). 427
  • Diagnostic pre-treatment tumor marker in thyroid cancer (keyed) → calcitonin (medullary); thyroglobulin is for follow-up after total thyroidectomy in differentiated cancer. 437 Final ×2
  • Firm fixed posterior-triangle neck swelling in an old lady: source key thyroid nuclear scan, but the compilers thought CT neck — see explanation. 426
Notes

10. Cancer Diagnosis

SEQUENCE RULE
Do not stage before confirming diagnosis when tissue confirmation is required. Suspicious lesion → imaging → biopsy/tissue diagnosis → confirm malignancy → staging.

Diagnostic modalities depend on the cancer: ultrasound, CT, MRI, upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy.

Notes

BI-RADS — Diagnostic Risk Stratification (breast)

CategoryMeaning
0Incomplete/not assessable → additional imaging required
1Negative
2Benign
3Probably benign → short-interval follow-up
4Suspicious abnormality
5Highly suggestive of malignancy
6Biopsy-proven malignancy
  • Histological Diagnosis: Obtaining tissue
  • Types of biopsy:
    • Incisional biopsy → Remove part of the lesion.
  • Excisional biopsy → Remove the entire lesion.
  • Core needle biopsy → Obtain a tissue core while preserving architecture.
  • Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) → Primarily obtains cells for cytological assessment.
Notes

11. Biopsy

TypeDescription
IncisionalRemoves part of the tumor; diagnostic, not definitive treatment
ExcisionalRemoves the entire lesion; may also be definitive treatment for a small, appropriately selected lesion
Core needleObtains a tissue core — preserves architecture, more histologic information
PunchUsed for selected superficial lesions
EndoscopicSamples mucosa/submucosa during endoscopy
FNAObtains cells only (cytology); limited architecture — gives cell type only, not full histologic detail
MYTH
The old belief that biopsy routinely causes cancer dissemination is incorrect.
  • Parathyroid cancer: the sample is taken as frozen section at surgery (FNA is avoided — risk of seeding). 435
  • Submucosal gastric mass with normal mucosa and central ulceration, presenting with hematemesis → GIST (CD117). 436
  • Thyroid nodule on exam/US → next step FNA. 427

Surgical Oncology: Histopathology

  • Confirm malignancy:
    • Benign vs malignant
  • Histological type:
    • Adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, sarcoma, etc.
  • Differentiation / grade:
    • Well, moderately, poorly differentiated when assessable
  • Tumor subtype:
    • e.g., mucinous adenocarcinoma
  • IHC profile:
    • helps determine tumor lineage and likely primary origin
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis + rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre → thyroid lymphoma. 435
  • Malignant lung tumor among the options: carcinoid. 427
Notes

What Is Assessed from the Biopsy?

1 Benign vs malignant

1.

2 Histologic type (adenocarcinoma, squamous carcinoma, lymphoma, sarcoma...)

2.

3 Degree of differentiation

3.

4 Tumor subtype

4.

5 Immunohistochemistry / molecular features when needed

5.

  • H. pylori carries the risk of upper GI contamination and neoplasia (commonest cause of peptic ulcer and gastric adenocarcinoma). 431 ×3
  • Immunohistochemistry (IHC):
    • Antibodies are used to detect specific proteins in tumor tissue.
  • Main purposes:
    • Identify tumor type → Cytokeratin (carcinoma), CD45 (lymphoma)
      • Identify primary origin → CDX2/SATB2 (colorectal), PAX8 (renal/Müllerian)
      • Guide treatment → ER/PR/HER2
      • Assess proliferation → Ki-67
      • Detect molecular pathway abnormalities → MMR proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6)
      • Assist sarcoma diagnosis → CD117/DOG1 (GIST)
Notes

12. Immunohistochemistry (IHC)

IHC detects specific proteins within tissue — identifies tumor lineage, likely site of origin, guides treatment, and provides prognostic information.

MarkerSupports
CytokeratinCarcinoma
CD45Lymphoid tumors / lymphoma
CDX2 / SATB2GI / colorectal origin
ER, PR, HER2 (breast)Suitability for hormone/targeted therapy
CANCER OF UNKNOWN PRIMARY (CUP)
Metastatic lesion found but routine imaging/endoscopy cannot show the primary (primary may be too small to detect) → biopsy the metastatic site (e.g. liver/peritoneum) → use an IHC panel to estimate origin. Molecular profiling may further guide systemic treatment.
IHC markerCommon association / use
CK7Common in breast, lung, ovarian, pancreatobiliary and urothelial tumors
CK20Common in colorectal and urothelial tumors
CDX2Intestinal / colorectal differentiation
SATB2Colorectal / appendiceal origin
TTF-1Lung adenocarcinoma and thyroid tumors
PAX8Renal, thyroid and Müllerian tumors
ER / PRBreast and gynecologic tumors; also predictive markers for hormonal therapy
HER2Breast and selected gastric/GEJ and other cancers; predictive for targeted therapy
PSA / NKX3.1Prostatic origin
SynaptophysinNeuroendocrine differentiation
Chromogranin ANeuroendocrine differentiation
S100 / SOX10Melanocytic and neural differentiation
Melan-A / HMB45Melanoma / melanocytic tumors
CD117 (KIT)GIST
DesminSmooth-muscle differentiation, e.g. leiomyosarcoma

Surgical Oncology: Staging

  • Complete staging work up (cancer specific)
    • Local staging
      • Distant metastasis
  • Clinical staging:
    • TNM: most of solid tumor
      • FIGO: Ovarian / cervical / endometrial cancer
      • WHO: Brain tumors
  • Purposes of staging:
    • Define the extent of disease
      • Assess likely prognosis
      • Allow the development of a treatment plan
  • Multidisciplinary Team discussion
Notes

13. Cancer Staging

Staging follows diagnosis/tissue confirmation. Purpose: determine extent of disease, identify local/regional/distant spread, estimate prognosis, guide treatment.

TNM = most common staging system for solid tumors. FIGO is used for many gynecologic cancers; brain tumors use specialized/WHO-based classifications. Staging investigations vary by cancer — common general imaging is CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (CT CAP); e.g. gastric cancer may need diagnostic laparoscopy ± PET.
  • Colon (splenic-flexure) adenocarcinoma → staging by CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. 429 Final
  • Biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinoma → next step CT scan (staging) — EUS and diagnostic laparoscopy come after. 433 Final
  • Staging colon cancer = CT chest, abdomen & pelvis. 427
Notes

Example: Rectal Cancer T Stage

StageExtent of invasion
T1Submucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Beyond muscularis propria into mesorectal/perirectal tissue (depth matters)
T4aPenetrates the visceral peritoneal surface
T4bDirectly invades adjacent organs/structures
PROGNOSTIC NOTE
Advanced T4 disease carries a high recurrence risk even with negative nodes.
  • Sentinel node biopsy in breast cancer = to assess the extent of lymphatic (axillary) involvement. 441

Surgical Oncology: MDT

  • Resectability: Can the tumor technically and oncologically be completely removed?
  • Operability: fitness for surgery → Can the patient safely tolerate the proposed operation?
  • Cancer factors + Patient factors + Treatment options: MDT decision
Notes

14. MDT, Resectability & Operability

After staging, cases are discussed at MDT/tumor board, integrating cancer factors, patient factors, functional status/comorbidities, and available treatment modalities.

DO NOT CONFUSE
Resectable: tumor can technically be completely removed surgically.
Unresectable: tumor cannot currently be completely removed — may receive treatment to convert to resectable, or palliation. Operable: the patient is physiologically/functionally fit for the proposed operation.
A tumor may be resectable but the patient inoperable due to poor functional status/comorbidity.

MDT may choose: surgery first, chemotherapy first, radiation first, combined treatment, or palliative management.

Surgical Oncology: TNM Staging

Surgical Oncology: Staging

Notes

15. Routes & Patterns of Cancer Spread

Main routes: hematogenous, lymphatic, direct local invasion, transcoelomic/peritoneal dissemination.

Primary tumorTypical spread pattern
Most intra-abdominal GI tumorsPortal venous drainage → liver is a common hematogenous site
Rectal cancer (lower)Venous drainage via iliac veins → lung metastases can occur without liver metastases
Renal / retroperitoneal tumorsSystemic venous drainage → lung common
Prostate cancerBone
Breast cancerBone, lung, brain
Renal cell carcinomaLung / bone
Ovarian cancerPeritoneal spread, may involve pleura
Testicular cancerRetroperitoneal lymph nodes
Gastric cancerOvary (Krukenberg tumor); left supraclavicular (Virchow) node
CLINICAL PEARL
Male patient with a retroperitoneal mass → examine the testes/scrotum for testicular cancer.

Surgical Oncology: TNM Staging

Surgical Oncology: Surgical management

  • Curative Surgery:
    • Complete removal of the cancer with adequate margins and appropriate regional lymph- node management while preserving function whenever possible.
  • Oncological resection
  • En-bloc resection
  • Resection margins:
    • R0 → no microscopic residual tumor
      • R1 → microscopic residual tumor
      • R2 → macroscopic residual tumor
  • Cytoredutive surgery?
Notes

16. Surgical Management

Curative / Oncologic Resection

Goal: complete radical resection with negative margins + appropriate lymph-node harvest — removing the tumor-bearing organ, relevant vascular/lymphatic drainage, and regional nodes.

EN BLOC RESECTION
Tumor + directly involved adjacent organ(s) removed together, without cutting through the tumor plane. Example: colon cancer invading bladder/uterus → resect the involved organ together with the colon rather than peeling the tumor away.
  • Palliative Surgery:

Surgery may be performed without an expectation of curing the cancer, with the goal of relieving symptoms or preventing major complications.

  • Obstructing unresectable colorectal cancer → diverting colostomy or bypass
  • Unresectable gastric cancer causing obstruction → gastrojejunostomy
  • Other indications include:
    • Bleeding
      • Obstruction
      • Perforation
      • Pain
      • Infection
  • Obstructing rectosigmoid/low rectal cancer with liver and lung metastases → diverting stoma (transverse colostomy). 435 ×2 437
  • "When is she cured?" → a normal duration of life without further clinical or radiological evidence of cancer. 439
Notes

Resection Margins

MarginMeaning
R0No residual tumor — microscopically negative margin (goal of complete oncologic resection)
R1Microscopic residual tumor / positive microscopic margin
R2Macroscopic residual tumor
Palliative Surgery / Intervention
• Palliative resection of obstructing tumor
• Stent for obstruction
• Diverting stoma
• Feeding tube (e.g. gastric malignancy)
• Pain-control procedures
• Diversion/bypass for obstruction		Goal = symptom control and quality of life, not cancer eradication — important even with metastatic/unresectable disease.
  • 89-year-old, obstructing sigmoid cancer with liver + lung metastases: source key colectomy (palliative resection) — see the explanation for the debate. 439
Notes

17. Multimodal Cancer Treatment

Cancer treatment is usually multimodal: surgery, chemotherapy/systemic therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, hormonal/endocrine therapy, radiotherapy, and local/regional therapies such as RFA for selected liver lesions.

Notes

Treatment Timing / Intent

TermDefinition
NeoadjuvantTreatment before surgery
AdjuvantTreatment after surgery
PerioperativeTreatment both before and after surgery
Definitive therapyIntended to provide curative control without another planned definitive modality
Curative intentAims to eradicate cancer
Palliative treatmentAims to control symptoms/disease and improve quality of life
Maintenance therapyLower-intensity, prolonged therapy to maintain control and delay progression
MODERN MULTIMODAL EXAMPLES
Melanoma: immunotherapy can produce major/complete responses in selected patients — has markedly changed management.
Rectal cancer — TNT (total neoadjuvant therapy): chemotherapy + radiotherapy before planned surgery, with approximately 30–40% complete clinical response, allowing selected patients to avoid immediate resection under close surveillance (requires intensive colorectal follow-up).
  • Why operate on incurable cancer? To improve quality of life. 439 ×2
  • Chemotherapy after resection = adjuvant. 435
  • Neoadjuvant radiotherapy role in rectal cancer → down-stage the tumor 436; neoadjuvant radiotherapy = local control. 435 ×2
Notes

18. Surveillance After Cancer Treatment

Every cancer has a specific surveillance program: history, exam, tumor markers, imaging, endoscopy, and organ-specific investigations (e.g. breast MRI, lung imaging, ultrasound). Any new clinical suspicion of recurrence warrants additional targeted investigation regardless of routine schedule.

TIMING
Colorectal cancer: recurrence is concentrated early — approximately 95% within 2 years, nearly all by ~3 years; by 5 years intensive surveillance is usually greatly reduced/completed.
Some slow-growing tumors, including selected sarcomas, may recur late → surveillance may extend to ~10 years.
Notes

19. Surgical Margins in Selected Soft-Tissue Tumors

Required safety margin depends on pathology. A benign lipoma generally needs no wide oncologic margin. Malignant soft-tissue tumors such as sarcoma / dermatofibrosarcoma may require ~2–4 cm margins depending on tumor/site. Inadequate margin → may require re-excision.

Surgical Oncology: Multimodal Treatment

  • Adjuvant chemotherapy role = local and metastatic (systemic) control. 439
  • Wait ~3 weeks after oncologic resection before chemotherapy (proliferative phase of wound healing). 435 · 438 Final ×6
  • Treatment timing:
    • Neoadjuvant therapy: before definitive surgery
      • Adjuvant therapy: after surgery
      • Perioperative therapy: before and/or after surgery
      • Definitive therapy: treatment intended as the primary curative modality
      • Palliative therapy: symptom control/prolongation of life
  • Local and Regional Therapies:
    • Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
      • Microwave ablation (MWA)
      • Cryoablation
      • Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE)

Cancer Surveillance

  • Planned follow-up after completion of cancer treatment to detect recurrence or new cancers.
  • Surveillance may include:
    • History & physical examination
      • Tumor markers
      • Imaging
      • Endoscopy
      • organ-specific tests
      • Further investigation if recurrence suspected
  • CEA = tumor marker of colorectal cancer, most useful for surveillance of recurrence (not screening). 436 441 437 ×2 436
  • Suspected brain tumor: initial investigation CT (old key; MRI is the definitive study). 427

Cancer Surveillance: Colon Cancer

  • Ulcerative colitis definitely increases colon cancer risk (more than Crohn's in this old question). 427

Summary: Strategy for cancer treatment

  • Possible neoadjuvant therapy to render primary cancer operable
  • Radical surgery for primary cancer
  • Treatment of lymph nodes: radical excision (e.g., gastric cancer) or lymph node sampling (e.g., breast cancer)
  • Adjuvant therapy based on pathologic staging after surgery (e.g., chemotherapy for lymph node metastases)
  • Radical surgery for distant metastases (e.g., excision of liver or lung metastases)
  • Palliative surgery for the relief of symptoms if no cure possible
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Neoplasia is unregulated and irreversible; hyperplasia is regulated and reversible when the stimulus is removed.
2 Carcinoma in situ stays above the basement membrane; invasive carcinoma breaches it.
3 Undifferentiated/anaplastic tumors carry the worst prognosis.
4 Somatic mutations are tumor-only; germline mutations are present throughout the body and are tested in blood/normal tissue.
5 Lynch syndrome (MSI/MMR deficiency) predisposes to colorectal plus ovarian/pancreatic cancers — family history may be absent.
6 Know the tumor-marker table cold: CEA–colorectal, CA 19-9–pancreatobiliary, CA-125–ovarian, AFP–HCC, PSA–prostate, calcitonin–medullary thyroid.
7 Diagnostic sequence is always imaging → biopsy → staging — never stage before tissue confirmation.
8 FNA gives cells only (cytology); core/excisional biopsy preserves tissue architecture for full histology.
9 Resectable vs operable are independent: a resectable tumor can still be in an inoperable patient.
10 R0 = microscopically clear margin (goal); R1 = microscopic residual disease; R2 = macroscopic residual disease.
11 En bloc resection removes involved adjacent organs together, never through the tumor plane.
12 Neoadjuvant = before surgery; adjuvant = after surgery.
13 Colorectal cancer recurrence is concentrated in the first 2–3 years; sarcomas may recur out to ~10 years.
14 Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumor, and Virchow node are classic exam signs of metastatic spread.
  • HCC paraneoplastic syndromes: hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypercholesterolemia, erythrocytosis — not hyperglycemia. 426
Beyond the slides

Other organ facts asked under oncology

  • Esophageal cancer predispositions: achalasia, Plummer-Vinson, Barrett's, corrosives — esophageal cyst is NOT precancerous. 427 426
  • Esophageal cancer: most common symptom is progressive dysphagia. 426
  • Barrett's esophagus predisposes to adenocarcinoma; it is not resected in the metaplasia phase (surveillance). 426
  • Benign esophageal tumors: leiomyoma, fibrovascular polyp, papilloma — leiomyosarcoma is malignant. 426
  • Palliation in esophageal cancer: stents, radiotherapy/brachytherapy, chemo (incomplete old question). 426
  • Paget's disease of the nipple = superficial manifestation of an underlying breast cancer. 426
  • Fibroadenoma: usually < 5 cm and well encapsulated ("large >5 cm, not capsulated" are wrong). 426
  • Cholangiocarcinoma is most common at the bifurcation of the hepatic ducts (Klatskin). 426
  • Liver lesions: metastases are the commonest malignant liver lesion (incomplete question). 426
  • Parotid malignant feature: skin ulceration (also facial nerve palsy, fixity). 426
  • Marjolin ulcer → SCC arising in a chronic scar/burn. 426
  • Commonest melanoma type: superficial spreading. 427
  • Picture of an ulcerated skin lesion → SCC. 435
